title: A disputed ode
hookLine: a well-known ode says "I am neither Christian nor Jew nor Muslim"; scholars doubt Rumi wrote it
tomorrow: the cover line says 'come, come, whoever you are.' is that Rumi?
last: WHAT DID I LOSE BY DYING?

lines: NOT CHRISTIAN, NOT JEW, NOT MUSLIM.
cards: Screenshots travel fast, and a well-known name travels faster. Zoe's friend Inés lost her grandmother last week, and Inés wants one poem on the back of the memorial program: an ode signed Rumi.
The speaker cries out, what is to be done, O Muslims? I don't know myself. I'm not Christian, not Jew, not Muslim.
Not of the East, not of the West. Then Inés's aunt texts one line. Where is that from?

teach.h: A REAL ODE, A DOUBTFUL NAME.
teach.b: Here's the honest answer. The ode is real and old.
Reynold Nicholson put it into English in his book of poems from Rumi's Divan, and the speaker sheds every label until all that's left is a placeless place, and two worlds seen as one.
But scholars who later edited the Divan from its older copies left this ode out. They doubt Rumi wrote it. A beautiful poem, a doubtful name.
Now the teaching, and it comes from Rumi's own world.

teach.h: ISNAD: WHO HEARD IT FROM WHOM.
teach.b: Muslim scholars built a whole discipline around one question: who said this, and who heard it from whom? It's called the isnad, the chain of a saying.
Before a word was credited to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, they traced the chain link by link and graded it.

teach.h: ENOUGH OF A LIE TO PASS ON EVERYTHING.
teach.b: In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, there's a warning from the Prophet: it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears.

teach.h: THE CHAIN IS PART OF THE RELIGION.
teach.b: And the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said the chain is part of the religion; without it, anyone could say whatever they liked.

Rumi was trained as a scholar in that world. So checking a Rumi line isn't doubting Rumi. It's treating his words the way his tradition treated words that mattered: loved enough to ask where they came from.

how: Hadith scholars grade a saying by its isnad, the chain of people who passed it on. Careful readers of Rumi check a line against critical editions of the Divan and the Masnavi before crediting it to him.

o: a short poem written to be read at a memorial
a poem credited to a poet who may not have written it
a poem banned for what it said about religion

editors who worked from the older copies of the Divan left this ode out; they doubt it's his.

a poem can be beautiful and still need the right name. love it, and ask.

games.q: a coworker posts a kind saying 'from the Prophet Muhammad.' you'd like to share it too. what would a hadith scholar do first?
o: share it; a kind line can't hurt anyone.
ask who passed it on, and check the chain.

games.why: the isnad: trace who heard it from whom. Sahih Muslim's introduction warns that passing on everything you hear is enough of a lie.

practice: Write one line you love by hand, a quote you'd put on a card or a wall. Under it, write the name you've always heard with it, and add a small question mark beside the name.
Let it sit there through the quiet; the line stays yours either way.

wordCard.voice: A disputed ode: a poem long printed under Rumi's name that his careful editors doubt is his. Beautiful, and unsettled.

orig.note: Arabic: the chain of a saying, the list of who passed it on. A word from Rumi's world, not from his poems.

carryVoice: Your line: check the source, the way scholars in Rumi's world checked a chain. Three days into Rumi again.
